<reason>Side A (CON) had the livelier voice and a genuinely clever central move: that every safeguard PRO offers (central purchase, free release on clinical need, caps) works by neutralising the high price, so the high price is pure rent, plus the "recoverable vs. un-grantable anchor" asymmetry. But that move partly self-destructs, and Side B (PRO) exploited it precisely. Once A concedes the unit price "does no allocative work" and is "a number on a ledger," it becomes very hard to justify a categorical veto keyed to unit price — which is exactly B's framing (value/total-cost test, not unit-price test). B also flipped A's central burden demand: A insisted PRO show a developer would walk away at an affordable price; B answered honestly that this is a mechanism claim, then pointed out symmetrically that A's whole rule presupposes an equivalent cheaper bargain that A never established, and that restructuring the payment need not reduce the public bill. B's Q1 also usefully defused A's "this is really a subscription" reframe: A answered "nothing — the label was never the issue," conceding that a guaranteed purchase at a high manufacturer price with free hospital distribution is still the very instrument the motion permits. B's closing dilemma on "revisit the terms" (either you eventually accept a justified high price, conceding the motion, or the ban leaves the gap unfilled and "nothing lost but time" understates the cost of delayed development) crystallised the clash most cleanly. A's cap-arithmetic rationing point was its best surviving damage, but B answered it coherently (reject inadequate coverage; permission is not obligation). A also incurred two clipped-speech execution costs on the opening and second rebuttal, losing its closing lines twice.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's handling of A's "pay twice / pure rent" line: by insisting the test is total public payment and value rather than per-course price, and noting that A's alternative payment structure does not necessarily lower the bill, B turned A's own concession that unit price is merely "a number on a ledger" into a reason not to veto on unit price at all.</best_rebuttal>
